nameStory: Syneilesis gets its name from Greek words meaning 'to wrap together,' referring to how the young leaves emerge tightly rolled up like little umbrellas. The species name 'aconitifolia' means 'with leaves like Aconitum' - the monkshood plant - because of the deeply divided, palmate leaf shape that resembles those poisonous beauties.
description: Syneilesis is an unusual member of the sunflower family that looks nothing like a typical daisy or aster. This perennial herb grows 2-4 feet tall with distinctive umbrella-like leaves that emerge in spring completely rolled up, then unfurl to reveal deeply divided, palmate leaves. The small, whitish flower clusters appear in summer but are quite inconspicuous compared to the dramatic foliage. It's an extremely rare plant in New England, with only one confirmed observation in our region.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, deeply palmately divided leaves that emerge rolled up like closed umbrellas in spring, then unfurl to show 7-9 pointed lobes with serrated edges. The leaves feel somewhat rough and have prominent veining.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 2-4 feet tall in clumps, with leaves on long stalks rising directly from the ground or short stems. The overall appearance is more like a large woodland wildflower than a typical aster.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous whitish or pale pink flower heads clustered at the top of tall stems in mid to late summer. Each tiny flower head lacks the obvious petals you'd expect from the sunflower family.

idTips.label: Leaves - Texture
idTips.description: Mature leaves have a slightly rough, papery texture when you run your fingers across them, and they make a soft rustling sound when disturbed by wind.

habitat: In its native Asian range, Syneilesis grows in moist, shaded woodland areas and forest edges. The single New England observation suggests it may occasionally escape cultivation or naturalize in similar rich, moist woodland soils. Look for it in areas with deep leaf litter and partial to full shade, possibly near gardens where it might have been planted as an ornamental.

seasonality.spring: The most exciting time to spot Syneilesis - watch for the distinctive tightly rolled umbrella-like leaf buds emerging from the soil, slowly unfurling as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are fully expanded and at their most impressive size. Small, inconspicuous flower clusters may appear on tall stalks above the foliage in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back. Seeds develop but are tiny and easily missed among the fading flower clusters.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground traces until the next spring's dramatic leaf emergence.

funFact: Syneilesis leaves emerge from the ground looking like tiny closed umbrellas or furled parasols, earning it the nickname 'umbrella plant' in Asia - but unlike a real umbrella opening, these leaves unfurl in slow motion over several weeks, creating one of the most dramatic leaf displays in the plant kingdom.
confusionNotes: The deeply divided leaves might be confused with wild ginger or some ferns when emerging, but the umbrella-like rolling pattern is unique. Once mature, the palmate leaves could resemble some Astilbe species, but Syneilesis has much more deeply cut leaf divisions and the distinctive emergence pattern.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is native to Asia and is extremely rare in New England - you're much more likely to encounter it in a specialty garden than in the wild. It's sometimes grown as an ornamental for its dramatic foliage, but it's not commonly available in garden centers.
compareHints: Syneilesis is the only species in its genus found in New England. Within the sunflower family, it's most similar to some of the unusual woodland asters, but none of them have the distinctive umbrella-like leaf emergence or deeply palmately divided leaves. The closest comparison might be with Cacalia species (Indian plantains), which also have unusual leaves for the sunflower family, but their leaves are much less divided and emerge normally rather than rolled up.
